summary: MXenes are ultrathin, layered nanomaterials with enormous surface area that can capture climate-warming CO2 from air or exhaust while ignoring other gases like nitrogen. Researchers describe how they are made, how they could be applied as paints or filters, and how captured CO2 might be released or converted into fuels. Challenges remain, including oxidation, small batch sizes, high cost and carbon footprint, and untested durability, so MXenes can supplement but not replace emission cuts.
one_line: Ultrathin MXene nanomaterials can sponge up CO2 from air or exhaust, but cost, durability and production challenges remain before real-world use.
key_facts: MXenes are nano-scale materials made of alternating layers of M (a transition metal) and X (carbon or nitrogen) atoms; each sheet is about 1 nanometer thick, roughly 100,000 times thinner than a sheet of paper.
One gram (1/400 ounce) of MXene has a total surface area that "can cover a football field," according to Per Persson of Linköping University in Sweden.
Persson's group has shown that MXenes can sponge up as much as half their weight in CO2, and MXenes chemically ignore other gases such as nitrogen.
MXenes do not exist in nature; they are made by using a strong acid such as hydrofluoric acid to etch away the A layers of lab-made MAX phases.
Safer methods use milder acids or bases such as sodium hydroxide, or molten fluoride salts, which need temperatures up to 750° Celsius (1,380° Fahrenheit).
Michael Naguib of Tulane University made the world's first MXene in 2011, a titanium carbide; scientists have now made more than 50 MXenes.
Mixed with water, MXene powder becomes an ink that can be painted onto fabric, plastic or glass, and MXene films toughened with polymers can separate CO2 from exhaust gas.
Persson imagines MXene filters atop chimneys, while Anupma Thakur suggests MXene screens in the open air, which would be less efficient because ambient CO2 levels are low.

Captured CO2 could be released by heating MXenes or flushing them with a gas such as hydrogen, and MXenes' catalytic properties could help turn CO2 into methanol or formic acid, according to Vitalie Stavila.
MXenes can break down into oxides in the presence of oxygen, and labs can currently make only several kilograms in one batch.
Making MXenes is costly and can carry a large carbon footprint because of the electricity needed for heat, and no one has yet tested their durability for repeated CO2 capture and release.
An October 4, 2023 paper in Chem by UC Riverside engineers led by Mihri Ozkan reviewed MXenes' potential and also pointed to related boron-based MBenes, mostly studied with computer models so far.
Human activities release tens of billions of tons of CO2 each year, so carbon absorbers cannot replace reducing emissions.
